"Yardarm" is a sailing and nautical word. To understand it, you first need to picture an old-fashioned sailing ship — the kind with tall masts and large fabric sails. This word describes a specific part of that ship.

On a sailing ship, a yard (or "yardarm's parent structure") is a long, horizontal wooden pole that is attached to the mast — the tall vertical pole at the center of the ship. This horizontal pole crosses the mast roughly at a right angle, like a giant "T" or a cross. Sails hang down from it.

Think of it like this: if the mast is the vertical bar of a cross, the yard is the horizontal bar.

A yardarm is either of the two outer ends of a yard — the tips that stick out to the left and right of the mast.

So the yard is the entire long horizontal pole. The yardarm is specifically the outermost portion of that pole, on either side. Each yard has two yardarms: one on the left side (port) and one on the right side (starboard).

Picture it: a mast goes up vertically. A long pole goes through it horizontally. The far-left tip of that pole is a yardarm. The far-right tip is also a yardarm.
How It Was Actually Used on a Ship

In the age of sail (roughly 1400s–1800s), yardarms served several real purposes:

  1. Supporting sails. The sails were attached to the yard and hung below it. The yardarms defined the full width of that sail area.
  2. Flying signals. Flags, signal lights, and pennants were often hoisted up to the yardarm to communicate with other ships — since the ends of the yard were high up and visible from far away.
  3. Rigging work. Sailors would sometimes have to climb out to the yardarm — a dangerous job — to handle ropes and sails in all kinds of weather.
The Dark Historical Use: Hanging from the Yardarm

One of the most historically significant uses of the yardarm was as a place of execution at sea.

When a sailor committed a serious crime — such as mutiny (rebelling against the captain), desertion, or piracy — the punishment could be death by hanging. Because there were no gallows on a ship, a rope would be tied to the yardarm, and the condemned person would be hanged from that high outer tip of the horizontal pole.

This was done because the yardarm was:

  • High enough off the deck to serve as a gallows
  • Visible to the entire crew, making the punishment a warning to others
  • Already a sturdy, load-bearing structure

This is why you'll often encounter the phrase "hanged from the yardarm" or "hang from the yardarm" in historical novels, sea stories, and expressions referring to punishment or doom.

Example: "The captain warned that any man who betrayed the ship would be hanged from the yardarm before sunrise."
The Famous Idiom: "The Sun Is Over the Yardarm"

This is the most commonly used expression involving "yardarm" in modern English, and it's worth knowing well.

Meaning: It is late enough in the day that it is socially acceptable to have an alcoholic drink.

Origin: On ships sailing in northern latitudes, the sun — when low on the horizon in the morning — was below the level of the yardarm when viewed from the deck. As the day progressed and the sun climbed higher in the sky, it would eventually rise above the yardarm. This moment (roughly mid-to-late morning, around 11 AM) was informally used by sailors as a signal that the working part of the morning was over and a drink was permissible.

Over time, this phrase moved from ships into everyday speech, where it is used humorously or casually to justify having a drink — especially during the day.

Example: "It's barely noon, but I suppose the sun is over the yardarm somewhere in the world." (Said when someone wants a drink earlier than is typically considered polite.)

Example: "Pour me a whiskey — the sun's well over the yardarm by now."

The phrase can also be used more broadly (and less literally) to mean simply: the right time has come for something.

Here are examples showing the word in different contexts:

  • Literal/nautical: "The sailor edged carefully along the yard and out to the yardarm to untangle the rigging during the storm."
  • Historical/punishment: "Pirates captured by the navy faced a swift trial and were hanged from the yardarm as a warning to others."
  • Idiomatic: "It's five o'clock — the sun is over the yardarm. Time for a drink."
  • Figurative/literary: "He felt as though he were dangling from the yardarm, waiting for the captain's verdict."

A yardarm is the outer end of a horizontal sailing pole (the yard) on a traditional sailing ship — historically used to hang condemned sailors, fly signal flags, and, by way of a famous idiom, to mark the time of day when it becomes acceptable to have a drink.
